ResStock 2025 Release 1 has five HVAC demand flexibility upgrades, numbers 24 to 28. They all adjust heating and cooling setpoints around a peak period. They differ in strategy, offset size and pre-peak duration.

| # | Upgrade | Strategy | Offset | Pre-peak duration |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 24 | HVAC Demand Flexibility with On-Peak Load Shedding of 2F offset | Shed load during the peak | 2°F | n/a |
| 25 | …with 4 hour Pre-peak Load Shifting of 2F offset | Shift load to before the peak | 2°F | 4 hours |
| 26 | …with On-Peak Load Shedding of 4F offset | Shed load during the peak | 4°F | n/a |
| 27 | …with 4 hour Pre-peak Load Shifting of 4F offset | Shift load to before the peak | 4°F | 4 hours |
| 28 | …with 1 hour Pre-peak Load Shifting of 2F offset | Shift load to before the peak | 2°F | 1 hour |

**How they differ**
- **Strategy:**
  - Upgrades 24 and 26 only shed load. They change setpoints during the on-peak period to cut heating and cooling use.
  - Upgrades 25, 27 and 28 shift load. They add a pre-peak window before the peak, which moves some HVAC energy earlier.
- **Offset size:** Upgrades 26 and 27 use the larger 4°F offset. Upgrades 24, 25 and 28 use 2°F. A larger offset should give more peak reduction but more occupant comfort impact.
- **Pre-peak length:** Upgrades 25 and 27 use a 4-hour pre-peak window. Upgrade 28 uses 1 hour.
- **Pairings:** Comparing 24 with 25 shows the effect of adding a 4-hour pre-peak window at 2°F. Comparing 25 with 28 shows the effect of window length. Comparing 25 with 27 shows the effect of offset size.

**Limits of what I found**
- The upgrade names and the setpoint-change description come from the ResStock [upgrade measures page](https://natlabrockies.github.io/ResStock.github.io/docs/upgrade_measures.html) and the [2025 R1 changelog](https://resstock.readthedocs.io/en/latest/changelog/changelog_2025_R1.html). The changelog says the feature "modifies the heating and cooling setpoint to reduce heating and cooling load during peak period."
- I couldn't read the linked measure documentation PDF, because it came back as unreadable binary. I therefore can't tell you the peak window hours, which seasons or equipment each upgrade applies to, or whether the shedding upgrades have any recovery or ramp behavior.
- I also don't know how the pre-peak step works. It is probably pre-cooling in cooling mode and pre-heating in heating mode, but that is my inference and not confirmed.
- The page lists the same documentation PDF, [93846.pdf](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy26osti/93846.pdf), for all five upgrades. You can open it directly for those details.

The ResStock team recommends **at least 1,000 samples** when nothing more specific is known. They say this limits uncertainty to about 15% when you draw conclusions from individual dwelling models.

- **Why 1,000:** The ResStock documentation says "ResStock recommends a minimum sample size of 1,000 for most applications to minimize the error."
- **What the samples represent:** Under quota sampling, every sample is weighted equally. In the 2022.1 dataset, 1,000 samples represent about 242,000 dwelling units.
- **When you need more:** The right number depends on what you're measuring, how variable those results are, and what the analysis is for. The team suggests estimating the standard error as the standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample count. You can use that to check whether your sample size is big enough.
- **The 350,000 figure:** This isn't a current recommendation. It comes from an older DOE study of single-family housing, and the buildstockbatch docs use it only as an example value for `n_datapoints`.

answer_text:
Yes, this is a documented known issue. The ResStock team lists it as [Wall Type Issue, Especially in Maine](https://natlabrockies.github.io/ResStock.github.io/docs/resources/explanations/Issue_Wall_Type_Especially_Maine.html) under [Limitations and Known Issues](https://natlabrockies.github.io/ResStock.github.io/docs/resources/resources.html).

**What's wrong**
- The Geometry Wall Type characteristic is wrong for Maine. The cause is the Maine portion of the county tax assessor dataset that ResStock uses to build wall type distributions.
- The team spot-checked against Zillow photos and found "considerable mislabeling of wall type." Zillow imports the same assessor data, so it shows the same errors.
- In the 2024 Release 2 data, Maine single-family detached homes come out at about 10% wood frame, 12% brick and 78% concrete block (CMU). That is the lowest wood-frame share of any state in that release. It also diverges from Vermont, which has similar housing, and from what local Maine building researchers know.
- The page says "We believe that all published ResStock datasets are impacted." The investigation is preliminary and no fix has been implemented.

**What it affects**
- The wall type and wall exterior finish characteristics are the main ones affected.
- Wall insulation is only minimally affected, because its option names include the wall type.
- Upgrade applicability is also affected. Measures that apply only to wood-frame walls will reach fewer Maine dwelling units than they should.
- The team doesn't currently believe energy consumption, emissions or energy bills are significantly affected, in either baseline or upgrade results.

**What to do if you need Maine wall type results**
- **Wall type or exterior finish distributions:** Don't use Maine's. Use results from nearby states, especially Vermont and New Hampshire.
- **Measures whose applicability depends on wall type:** Either reweight the Maine results using the nearby states' wall type distributions, or use the nearby states' results directly.
- **Energy, emissions or bills:** The team doesn't expect a significant problem. If wall type matters to your analysis, state the caveat anyway.

If you need more than this, the page points to resstock@nlr.gov for questions. Check the page again before you publish, since the team may have fixed the problem by then.

**The problem**
- ResStock gets its Geometry Wall Type characteristic from a nationally compiled county tax assessor dataset. The Maine records in that dataset mislabel wall types.

- Other states haven't shown the problem, but they haven't been checked comprehensively.

**Scope**
- The 2024 Release 2 dataset shows it, and the team believes all published ResStock datasets are affected.
- Wall Type and Wall Exterior Finish are directly affected. Insulation Wall is only minimally affected.
- Upgrades that apply only to wood-frame walls will reach fewer Maine dwelling units than they should.
- The team doesn't currently expect significant effects on energy consumption, emissions or bills, in either baseline or upgrade runs.
- A preliminary investigation is done and a detailed one is pending. No fix has been made.

**What to do for Maine wall type results**
1. For wall type or exterior finish distributions, use results from nearby states, especially Vermont or New Hampshire.
2. For measures whose applicability depends on wall type, either reweight the Maine results using nearby-state wall type distributions or use the nearby-state results directly.
